Boorish is an adjective used to describe a person or their behavior as rough, rude, and unpleasant — in a way that shows a complete lack of good manners, sensitivity, and social awareness. A boorish person makes others feel disrespected and uncomfortable simply by the way they behave.

Think of it this way: most people, when they are in social situations — a dinner, a meeting, a conversation — naturally try to be considerate. They listen when others speak, they speak with some degree of politeness, they read the room, and they avoid acting in ways that would make others cringe or feel small.

A boorish person does none of that. They bulldoze through social situations without any awareness of — or concern for — how their behavior affects others. They are loud, crude, dismissive, and graceless. And importantly, the word carries a sense that this rudeness comes not from occasional bad judgment, but from a deeply ingrained coarseness of character.
What Boorish Behavior Actually Looks Like

This is where the word truly comes to life. Boorish behavior includes things like:

  • Interrupting people constantly without any apology or awareness.
  • Making crude, offensive, or inappropriate jokes in serious or formal settings.
  • Talking loudly about yourself and showing no interest in others.
  • Being visibly rude or dismissive to waitstaff, service workers, or people considered "beneath" them.
  • Eating in a messy, loud, or repulsive way at the dinner table.
  • Using vulgar language in situations where it is clearly unwelcome.
  • Belching, being physically crude, or acting in ways most adults would consider deeply inappropriate in company.
  • Expressing opinions in a harsh, aggressive, or contemptuous way — with no care for how it lands.
  • Bragging, dominating conversations, and leaving others feeling invisible.

What ties all of these together is a single thread: a total disregard for the comfort, dignity, and feelings of the people around them.

Here is something subtle but important. A boorish person is not necessarily a cruel or malicious person. They are not plotting to hurt others. Very often, they are simply oblivious — they have never developed the social sensitivity to realize how grating and unpleasant their behavior is. They lack what you might call "social polish." However, even if it comes from ignorance rather than intention, the effect is the same: they make interactions with them genuinely unpleasant.

This is what separates boorish from a word like mean or malicious. A mean person wants to hurt you. A boorish person doesn't particularly care either way — and that indifference is exactly what makes them boorish.

Boorish is a strong, critical word. It is not a casual or mild complaint. When someone describes a person or their behavior as boorish, it is a serious negative judgment on their character and social conduct. It signals that the person in question falls significantly below the standard of decent, considerate behavior that is expected of adults in society.
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "His boorish behavior at the dinner party left everyone feeling embarrassed for him."
  • "She refused to tolerate his boorish remarks any longer and left the room."
  • "Despite being highly educated, he had a boorish manner that put people off immediately."
  • "The audience was uncomfortable with the comedian's boorish style of humor."
  • "His boorish attitude toward his colleagues made him deeply unpopular at work."

Notice that "boorish" can describe behavior, comments, attitudes, humor, or manner — it is flexible in how it attaches to things, as long as those things involve crude, inconsiderate, and socially unacceptable conduct.
Words Close to "Boorish" (and How They Differ)

Understanding where boorish sits among similar words will sharpen your sense of it.

Uncouth is the closest synonym. It similarly describes someone rough and lacking in refinement, but uncouth can sometimes feel slightly softer or more neutral — describing someone simply unfamiliar with social norms. Boorish carries a stronger sense of active social offensiveness.

Crude focuses specifically on coarseness — particularly in humor or language. A boorish person is often crude, but crude doesn't always imply the full social obnoxiousness that boorish does.

Loutish is very similar to boorish, but often suggests physical clumsiness or thuggishness alongside the rudeness — a big, clumsy, insensitive kind of rudeness.

Oafish implies rudeness mixed with a kind of stupidity or slow-wittedness.

Churlish focuses more specifically on being grumpy, unfriendly, and ungenerous — where boorish is broader, covering general social crudeness.

Vulgar zeros in on being offensive to good taste, particularly in a sexual or indecent sense. A boorish person may be vulgar, but boorish covers more ground.

The opposites of boorish help anchor its meaning further. A person who is the opposite of boorish might be described as:

Refined, courteous, gracious, well-mannered, cultured, polished, civil, or genteel.

These words all point to someone who moves through social situations with awareness, consideration, and elegance — the exact qualities a boorish person lacks entirely.

If you ever need to recall the essence of this word quickly:

Boorish describes a person or behavior that is rough, rude, crude, and inconsiderate — in a way that shows a clear and deep lack of good manners and social sensitivity, making the experience of being around that person genuinely unpleasant.
